questions.question: Which cookie flag stops an XSS script from reading the session cookie via document.cookie?
questions.explanation: httpOnly hides the cookie from client-side JavaScript. secure only restricts it to HTTPS, sameSite controls cross-site sending, and signing only detects tampering.

questions.question: Why is the default express-session MemoryStore unsuitable for production?
options: It leaks memory, loses sessions on restart and cannot be shared across multiple instances
It stores session data in the cookie, which the browser can read
It does not support the httpOnly flag
questions.explanation: MemoryStore lives inside one process. Production apps need a shared store such as Redis or a database so every instance can find every session and sessions survive restarts.

questions.question: What is the correct way to store user passwords?
options: Encrypt them with AES so they can be decrypted for support staff
Store them in a signed cookie
Hash them with a slow, salted algorithm such as bcrypt or argon2
questions.explanation: Fast hashes like SHA-256 can be brute-forced at enormous speed, and reversible encryption means a key leak exposes every password. bcrypt and argon2 are deliberately slow and embed a salt.

questions.question: Behind a TLS-terminating load balancer, your secure session cookie is never set. What is the most likely fix?
options: Configure app.set("trust proxy", ...) so Express recognises the original request as HTTPS
questions.explanation: Without trust proxy, Express sees the proxy's plain-HTTP request and refuses to send a secure cookie. Trusting the proxy lets it read X-Forwarded-Proto.
